abstract: Colibactin is a secondary metabolite produced by bacteria present in the human gut and is implicated in the development of colorectal cancer. This genotoxin alkylates deoxyadenosines on opposite strands of host cell DNA to produce DNA interstrand cross-links. While cells have evolved multiple mechanisms to resolve (“unhook”) interstrand cross-links, little is known about which of these pathways promote resistance to colibactin. Here, we use Xenopus egg extracts to investigate replication-coupled repair of colibactin-induced interstrand cross-links. We show that replication fork stalling at a colibactin-induced interstrand cross-link activates the Fanconi anemia interstrand cross-link repair pathway, which unhooks the interstrand cross-link through nucleolytic incisions. These incisions generate a DNA double-strand break intermediate in one sister chromatid, which can be repaired by homologous recombination, and a monoadduct (“interstrand cross-link remnant”) in the other. Translesion synthesis past the colibactin-induced interstrand cross-link remnant depends on Pol η and the Pol κ-REV1-Pol ζ polymerase complex and introduces predominantly T>A point mutations at the sites of colibactin alkylation. Taken together, our work provides a molecular framework for understanding how cells tolerate a naturally occurring and clinically relevant interstrand cross-link.

−1

−1

−1

−1

Replication reactions
Plasmid replication reactions in
Xenopus
egg extracts were performed essentially as previously described
62
. Briefly, HSS was thawed and supplemented with 20 mM phosphocreatine, 2 mM ATP, 5 µg mL
−1
creatine phosphokinase, and 3 µg mL
−1
nocodazole. Plasmids were added to the HSS mix to a concentration of 7.5 ng µL
−1
and incubated at room temperature for 30 min to enable licensing. For assays involving LacR acting as a replication block, plasmids were pre-incubated with 14 µM biotinylated LacI for 1 h at room temperature before being added to HSS. Where indicated, the licensing mix was supplemented with 167–333 nM 3000 Ci mmoL
−1
[α−
32
P]dCTP and/or 400 nM rGeminin. NPE mix was made with 50% NPE, 20 mM phosphocreatine, 2 mM ATP, 5 µg mL
-1
creatine phosphokinase, and 4 mM DTT in ELB. Where indicated, the NPE mix was with 50 µM PHA-767491 HCl or 300 µM NMS-873. Replication was initiated by the addition of 2 volumes of NPE mix to 1 volume of licensing mix. Where indicated, 10 mM IPTG was added 15 min into the replication time course to dissociate LacI from the plasmid. For samples analyzed by APE1 digestion, HSS and NPE mixes were combined before adding the plasmid (i.e., replication origins were not licensed in the HSS mix). For analysis on native agarose gels, 1 µL samples of the reaction were removed at indicated time points and quenched by addition to 6 µL of replication stop mix (80 mM Tris-HCl [pH 8.0], 8 mM EDTA, 0.13% phosphoric acid, 10% ficoll, 5% SDS, 0.1% bromophenol blue). After all time points were quenched, samples were digested with 1.25 mg mL
−1

Autoradiograms were imaged with a Typhoon FLA 9500 (GE Healthcare) using the FujiFilm FLA 9500 user interface v.1.1 and analyzed using Image Lab v.6.4.0. For Southern blots and nascent strand analysis on sequencing gels, 4 µL samples of the reaction were removed at indicated time points and quenched by addition to 40 µL of clear replication stop mix (50 mM Tris-HCl [pH 8.8], 0.5% SDS, 25 mM EDTA). After all time points were quenched, samples were digested with 200 µg mL
−1

−1

recombinant albumin; pH 7.9) in a total volume of 5 µL at 37 °C for 60 min. Following digestion, 5 µL of 50 mM Tris-HCl (pH 8.8), 50 mM NaCl, 10 mM EDTA, and 2 µL of 6X alkaline loading buffer (300 mM NaOH, 6 mM EDTA, 18% ficoll, 0.25% xylene cyanol, 0.15% bromocresol green) was added to each sample. The DNA was resolved on a denaturing 0.8% agarose, 50 mM NaOH, 1 mM EDTA gel for 20 h at 1.25 V cm
−1
. After running was complete, the gel was incubated in 0.25 M HCl for 20 min and in 0.4 M NaOH, 3 M NaCl for 60 min. Downward capillary transfer onto an Invitrogen BrightStar-Plus positively charged nylon membrane was performed overnight in 0.4 M NaOH, 1.5 M NaCl. The membrane was subsequently washed with 4X SSC buffer (0.6 M NaCl, 60 mM sodium citrate; pH 7.0) for 5 min, and the DNA was cross-linked to the membrane via 265 nm UV irradiation (120,000 µJ cm
−2
) with a UVP HybriLinker Oven. The membrane was then incubated with 15 mL ULTRAhyb Ultrasensitive Hybridization Buffer (Invitrogen) for 1–2 h at 42 °C. During this prehybridization, a radioactive probe was made using 50 ng of linearized pCtrl and the Prime-a-Gene Labeling System kit (Promega) following the manufacturer’s instructions. The probe was added to the hybridization tube and incubated with the membrane at 42 °C for 18 h. After hybridization, the membrane was washed twice with 1X SSC, 0.7% SDS at 42 °C for 10–20 min per wash and twice with 0.1X SSC, 0.7% SDS that was pre-heated to 75 °C for 10–20 min per wash. The membrane was dried briefly on blotting paper and visualized by phosphorimaging as described above.
Nascent strand analysis
Nascent strand analysis was performed essentially as previously described
36
. Briefly, samples were replicated as described above, and 2 µL of recovered DNA were incubated with 2 U AflIII and 4 U of either EcoRI or BamHI in 50 mM Tris-HCl (pH 8), 100 mM NaCl, 10 mM MgCl
2
in a total volume of 5 µL at 37 °C for 3 h. Reactions were stopped by adding 5 µL of Invitrogen Gel Loading Buffer II. Primers for sequencing ladders were radiolabeled by incubating 200 nM sequencing primer with 200 nM [γ−
32
P]ATP and 20 U T4 polynucleotide kinase (NEB) in 1X T4 PNK reaction buffer (70 mM Tris-HCl, 10 mM MgCl
2
, 5 mM DTT; pH 7.6) in a total volume of 50 µL for 30 min at 37 °C. T4 PNK was inactivated by heating at 95 °C for 2 min, and the unincorporated radionucleotides were removed using a Micro Bio-Spin column (Bio-Rad) per the manufacturer’s instructions. Sequencing ladders were made using the Thermo Sequenase Cycle Sequencing Kit: 0.5 pmol of radiolabeled primer mixed with 175 ng of pCtrl, 2 µL of reaction buffer, and 2 µL of Sequenase in a total volume of 17.5. 4 µL of this reaction mix was then added to 4 µL of ddA, ddG, ddC, or ddT termination mixes, and the reactions were incubated on a PCR block at 95 °C for 3 min, followed by 50 cycles of 95 °C for 30 s, 60 °C for 60 s, and 72 °C for 90 s. Eight microliters of Invitrogen Gel Loading Buffer II were added to each reaction, and the sequencing ladders were stored at −20 °C until use. Immediately before loading, all samples were heated at 75 °C for 5 min and snap-cooled in an ice water bath. DNA was resolved on a 7% acrylamide/bis (19:1), 8 M urea, 0.8X glycerol tolerant gel (GTG) buffer (71 mM Tris-HCl, 23 mM taurine, 0.4 mM EDTA) gel. Sequencing gels were dried and visualized by phosphorimaging as described above.
Plasmid pulldown and sample preparation for mass spectrometry
Plasmid pulldowns for the purpose of mass spectrometry were performed essentially as previously described
40
. Briefly, 6 µL of M-280 Streptavidin Dynabeads (Invitrogen) per time point were washed three times with 50 mM Tris-HCl (pH 7.5), 150 mM NaCl, 0.02% Tween-20, and 1 mM EDTA (pH 8.0) and subsequently incubated in the same buffer supplemented with 2 pmol of biotinylated LacI per µL of beads for 40 min at room temperature on a rotator wheel. The beads were washed four times with pulldown buffer (2.5 mM MgCl
2
, 50 mM KCl, 10 mM HEPES, 250 mM sucrose, 0.25 mg mL
−1
BSA, 0.02% Tween-20), divided into 40 µL aliquots, and stored on ice. Replication reactions were performed as described above, except extracts were supplemented with 40 µg mL
−1
RNAse A and 10 U µL
−1
RNAse T1, and plasmids were replicated at a final concentration of 5 ng µL
−1
in extracts. At the indicated times, 8 µL of each reaction was quenched into 40 µL of Dynabeads (with four replicates for each time point) and immediately incubated on a rotator wheel for 30 min at 4 °C to enable binding of the plasmid’s
lacO
array to the LacI-coated beads. After the incubation, the beads were washed twice at 4 °C with 2.5 mM MgCl
2
, 50 mM KCl, 10 mM HEPES, 250 mM sucrose, 0.03% Tween-20, and once with 2.5 mM MgCl
2
, 50 mM KCl, 10 mM HEPES, 250 mM sucrose. For each time point, the beads for one of the replicates were suspended in 10 µL of 1X Laemmli loading buffer and analyzed by immunoblotting. Beads for the other three replicates were suspended in 50 µL of 50 mM HEPES-KOH (pH 8.0), transferred to fresh microtubes, and stored on ice. The buffer was aspirated from the beads, and they were resuspended in 50 µL of 8 M urea in 50 mM HEPES-KOH (pH 8.0). Subsequent steps were performed at room temperature unless otherwise indicated. Samples were incubated with 20 mM DTT for 15 min, supplemented with chloroacetamide to 58 mM, and incubated at 1200 rpm on a Thermomixer for 40 min (covered in foil to protect from light). Samples were then incubated with 1.5 µg Lys-C at 1400 rpm on a Thermomixer for 150 min. Following the incubation, supernatants containing the eluted peptides were separated from the beads on a magnetic rack and transferred to fresh tubes (~60 µL of supernatant per sample). Samples were adjusted to 200 µL with 50 mM ammonium bicarbonate and incubated with 2.5 µg of trypsin at 30 °C overnight. Digestions were terminated by adding 20 µL of 10% TFA (trifluoroacetic acid) and adjusted to 0.5 M NaCl by adding 74 µL of 2 M NaCl. Stage tips were prepared by dispensing two C18 disks into 200 µL pipette tips with a blunt needle and spinning at 500 ×
g
for 3 min to pack the disks. All subsequent stage tip spins were also performed at 500 ×
g
for 3 min. Stage tips were activated by spinning with 100 µL 50% acetonitrile (ACN) and equilibrated by spinning with 100 µL 0.1% TFA. Samples were spun at 8000 ×
g
for 10 min to pellet any undigested DNA debris. Eighty-five microliters of supernatant were applied to stage tips and spun; this step was repeated two more times, leaving ~40 µL of each sample behind to avoid disturbing the pellet. Stage tips were washed twice with 100 µL of 0.1% TFA, and peptides were eluted twice with 50 µL of 50% ACN, 0.1% TFA. Samples were then dried in a SpeedVac, reconstituted in 10 µL of 2% ACN/0.2% FA (formic acid) solution, sonicated for 5 min, and centrifuged at 16,000 ×
g
for 5 min. Four microliters of each sample were transferred to autosampler vials. LC-MS/MS analysis was performed with an EASY-nLC 1200 (Thermo Fisher Scientific, San Jose, CA) coupled to a Q Exactive HF hybrid quadrupole-Orbitrap mass spectrometer (Thermo Fisher Scientific, San Jose, CA). Peptides were separated on an Aurora UHPLC Column (25 cm × 75 μm, 1.7 μm C18, AUR3-25075C18, Ion Opticks) with a flow rate of 0.35 μL min
−1
for a total duration of 75 min and ionized at 1.6 kV in the positive ion mode. The gradient was composed of 6% solvent B (3.5 min), 6–25% B (42 min), 25–40% B (14.5 min), and 40–98% B (15 min); solvent A: 2% ACN and 0.2% formic acid in water; solvent B: 80% ACN and 0.2% formic acid. MS1 scans were acquired at a resolution of 60,000 from 375 to 1500
m
/
z
, AGC target 3E6, and maximum injection time 15 ms. The 12 most abundant ions in MS2 scans were acquired at a resolution of 30,000, AGC target 1E5, maximum injection time 60 ms, and a normalized collision energy of 28. Dynamic exclusion was set to 30 s, and ions with charges of +1, +7, +8, and >+8 were excluded. The temperature of the ion transfer tube was 275 °C, and the S-lens RF level was set to 60.
Proteomic data processing
Label-free quantification (LFQ) of protein abundances was performed with the MaxLFQ algorithm implemented in MaxQuant (MQ v2.3.1.0)
63
–
65
. The analysis used default settings with match between runs functionality enabled. RAW data were searched against an in silico tryptic digested protein reference database based on the 10.1 version of the
Xenopus laevis
genome downloaded from Xenbase (
https://wuehr.scholar.princeton.edu/sites/g/files/toruqf2761/files/xenla_10_1_xenbase.fasta_.txt
). The maximum missed cleavages were set to 2. Dynamic modifications were set to oxidation on methionine (M, +15.995 Da) and protein N-terminal acetylation (+42.011 Da). Carbamidomethylation on cysteine residues (C, +57.021 Da) was set as a fixed modification. Protein quantification was performed using the built-in LFQ algorithm. The data have been deposited to the ProteomeXchange Consortium via the PRIDE partner repository with the dataset identifier PXD055646
66
.
The Perseus software platform (v.2.1.2.0) was used for data filtering and normalization
67
. Potential contaminant proteins, reverse database protein hits, proteins identified only by modification site, and proteins that were not quantified in at least one replicate group were removed from the analysis. LFQ intensities were log2-transformed, and samples were median-normalized. Missing abundance values were imputed from a downshifted normal distribution with default parameters defined in Perseus. For heatmap visualization, normalized abundances were averaged within biological replicate groups and standardized. The R package
limma
was used for statistical analysis of protein abundances
68
. Differential expression
p
values from empirical Bayes moderated t-testing of the log2-transformed protein ratios were adjusted for multiple hypothesis testing with the Benjamini-Hochberg procedure
69
.
Immunoblotting
Samples in 1X Laemmli loading buffer (generally corresponding to 1–2 µL of replication reaction or 9 µL of a plasmid pulldown sample) were resolved on 10% or 4–15% acrylamide Mini-PROTEAN or Criterion TGX precast gels (Bio-Rad) and transferred to polyvinyl difluoride (PVDF) membranes (Thermo Fisher). Membranes were blocked with 5% non-fat milk in 1X PBS buffer with 0.05% (v/v) Tween-20 (PBST) for 1 h at room temperature, rinsed four times with 1X PBST, and incubated with primary antibodies diluted to an appropriate concentration in 1X PBST at 4 °C overnight with shaking. Primary antibody dilutions were as follows: Rabbit polyclonal anti-MCM7 (
Xenopus
) Pocono Rabbit Farm and Laboratory rabbit 456, 1:12,000; Rabbit polyclonal anti-CDC45 (
Xenopus
) Pocono Rabbit Farm and Laboratory rabbit 534, 1:20,000; Rabbit polyclonal anti-H3 (human) Cell Signaling Technology catalog no. 9715S, 1:500; Rabbit polyclonal anti-REV1 (C terminus;
Xenopus
) Pocono Rabbit Farm and Laboratory rabbit 714, 1:5000; Rabbit polyclonal anti-FANCI (
Xenopus
) Pocono Rabbit Farm and Laboratory rabbit 26864, 1:5000; and Rabbit polyclonal anti-FANCD2 (
Xenopus
) Pocono Rabbit Farm and Laboratory rabbit 20019, 1:5000; Rabbit polyclonal anti-Pol η New England Peptide rabbit 2991, 1:5000, and Rabbit polyclonal anti-Pol κ New England Peptide rabbit 3924, 1:5000
52
. The next day, the membranes were washed with 1X PBST three times for 10 min each at room temperature, then incubated for 30 min at room temperature with goat anti-rabbit peroxidase-conjugate secondary antibody (IgG, H + L; Jackson ImmunoResearch catalog no. 111-035-003) diluted 1:25,000 in 1X PBST with 5% (w/v) non-fat milk. After the incubation, the membranes were again washed with 1X PBST three times for 10 min each at room temperature, then incubated with ProSignal Pico Spray chemiluminescence substrate (Prometheus) for 1–2 min at room temperature and imaged using a ChemiDoc Imaging System (Bio-Rad). Goat anti-rabbit peroxidase-conjugate secondary antibody (IgG, H + L) was manufacturer validated by antigen-binding assay, western blotting, and/or enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay. All antibodies against
Xenopus
proteins used in this study were validated by western blotting using
Xenopus
egg extracts.
Preparation of next-generation sequencing libraries
In preparation for NGS, plasmids were replicated as described above. After extraction and ethanol precipitation, samples were resuspended to a concentration of approximately 10–15 ng µL
−1
. Four microliters of recovered DNA were mixed with 200 nM each of forward and reverse primer (see Supplementary Table
1
), 200 µM dNTPs, and 2 units of Phusion High-Fidelity DNA Polymerase (NEB) in 1X Phusion HF buffer to a total volume of 100 µL. Amplicons were generated by PCR with initial heating to 98 °C for 30 s, followed by 18 cycles of 98 °C for 10 s, 55 °C for 30 s, and 72 °C for 30 s, and a final incubation at 72 °C for 10 min. The amplified DNA was purified with a QIAquick PCR Purification Kit (Qiagen) per the manufacturer’s instructions and inspected on a 0.8% agarose, 1X TBE gel visualized with SYBR Gold to confirm amplification. Samples were then submitted to Azenta for paired-end NGS (Illumina MiSeq, 2 × 250 bp).
NGS data processing
Raw sequencing reads were cropped to 150 bp using Trimmomatic (v0.39) to avoid later merging failures due to sequencing errors at the ends of amplicons
70
. Reads were then processed using SIQ (v1.8) with long-read analysis enabled and otherwise default settings, and the SIQPlotteR web tool was used to generate plots
71
. pICL
clb
contains a single C-C mismatch designed to distinguish reads derived from the two parental strands. These were not deconvoluted in our analysis; instead, the SBS corresponding to the C-C mismatch was manually removed from the SIQ output for pICL
clb
data sets.

Further information on research design is available in the
Nature Portfolio Reporting Summary
linked to this article.

Introduction
Human health is profoundly influenced by host-microbiome interactions. Emerging data indicate that pathogenic gut bacteria can contribute to dysbiosis and promote inflammation by producing toxins that damage host DNA
1
.
pks
+
bacteria harbor a 52-kilobase (kb) non-ribosomal polypeptide synthetase/polyketide synthase biosynthetic gene cluster that enables production of the colibactin genotoxin
2
. Colibactin-producing bacteria are detected in ~40% of patients with inflammatory bowel disease and ~60% of patients with colorectal cancer
3
. Moreover, colibactin exposure is associated with single-base substitution (SBS) and insertion/deletion mutational signatures found in the colonic crypts of most healthy individuals
4
–
6
. Colibactin is therefore a highly prevalent and potent driver of human disease.
Colibactin (clb) comprises a pseudo-
C
2
-symmetric scaffold with two cyclopropane groups (Fig.
1a
)
7
–
9
. Each cyclopropane can react with a deoxyadenosine (dA) to form a monoadduct or a DNA interstrand cross-link (ICL) that covalently links the two DNA strands. Consistently, clb-associated mutational signatures target AT-rich motifs containing offset dAs on opposite strands
5
,
6
,
10
. Once formed, the colibactin-ICL (clb-ICL) renders the alkylated dAs susceptible to depurination, resulting in an N3 monoalkylated base in one strand and a DNA abasic (AP) site in the other. The AP site can further decompose into a DNA strand break
11
. Shunt colibactin metabolites that have been isolated from
pks
+
mutated strains may also alkylate DNA
12
. Thus,
pks
+
bacteria likely generate a complicated spectrum of host DNA lesions that mobilize multiple DNA repair pathways.

EcoRI cuts 305 or 328 nt to the right of the c742-ICL or clb-ICL, respectively. Digestion with AflIII and EcoRI generates characteristic nascent strand −20 to −40 stall, −1 stall, and extension products. Right, DNA recovered from the pICL

and pICL

The clb-ICL is likely to be highly cytotoxic due to its presumed ability to stall replication forks. Failure to repair ICLs encountered during replication can lead to under-replication of the genome and/or gross chromosomal rearrangements. Consequently, cells have evolved multiple repair mechanisms that are activated when a replication fork encounters an ICL (Fig.
1b
)
13
. An ICL induced by acetaldehyde (AA-ICL) can be unhooked through direct reversal of the cross-link
14
. ICLs formed by psoralen or by AP sites can be unhooked by the NEIL3 DNA glycosylase, which excises a cross-linked base to produce an AP site
15
. Should these pathways fail, the ICL is unhooked by the Fanconi anemia (FA) pathway
13
. This pathway is activated when replicative CDC45-MCM2-7-GINS (CMG) helicases stall at an ICL
16
. CMGs are then polyubiquitylated by the replisome-associated TRAIP E3 ubiquitin ligase, leading to p97-dependent CMG unloading and reversal of one of the two converged forks
17
–
19
. At this stage, the FA core complex monoubiquitylates the FANCI-FANCD2 heterodimer, which becomes clamped onto DNA near the ICL
20
,
21
. Monoubiquitylated FANCI-FANCD2 recruits structure-specific nucleases, including XPF-ERCC1, that unhook the ICL through nucleolytic incisions flanking the ICL
22
. Following restoration of the reversed fork, one sister chromatid contains an ICL remnant that can be bypassed by the REV1-Pol ζ translesion synthesis (TLS) polymerase, while the other chromatid contains a DNA double-strand break (DSB) that is repaired by homologous recombination
23
,
24
. Importantly, the FA pathway is thought to be capable of unhooking any ICL, regardless of cross-link structure, and is therefore regarded as the most important pathway for cellular resistance to ICL-inducing agents. Consistent with this inference, mutations in any of 23 genes associated with this pathway cause a human bone marrow failure and cancer predisposition syndrome.
Despite the importance of the FA pathway for human health, the physiological ICLs targeted by this pathway remain obscure. Synergy between mutations in the FA pathway and mutations in aldehyde metabolism implies that the FA pathway resolves ICLs formed by endogenous aldehydes, such as formaldehyde or acetaldehyde
25
,
26
. Indeed, a chemically synthesized acetaldehyde-ICL is processed by the FA pathway in
Xenopus
egg extracts
14
. However, ICLs induced by acetaldehyde or any other endogenous metabolite have not been confirmed in vivo. Furthermore, FANC proteins have been shown to promote a variety of genome maintenance mechanisms in addition to ICL repair, including homologous recombination, replication fork protection, R-loop resolution, retrotransposon suppression, and mitochondrial genome maintenance
27
–
31
. Intriguingly, indirect evidence suggests that colibactin-induced ICLs might be repaired by the FA pathway. Colibactin exposure induces FANCD2 ubiquitylation and FANCD2 foci formation in cells, and FANCD2-deficient cells are hypersensitive to colibactin
32
. However, given the spectrum of DNA lesions produced during colibactin exposure and the multiple genoprotective functions of FANCD2, it remains unclear whether colibactin-induced ICLs are repaired by the FA pathway.
Here, we use
Xenopus
egg extracts to investigate replication-coupled repair of site-specific ICLs formed by either the native colibactin toxin or a synthetic colibactin analog. We find that both ICLs are strong impediments to DNA replication that trigger replication-coupled repair by the FA pathway. TLS past both an unhooked colibactin-induced ICL remnant and a colibactin monoadduct requires REV1 and Pol κ. We further show that colibactin-induced ICL repair can be error-free but frequently introduces primarily T>A point mutations. These results define the mechanisms that allow cells to tolerate a DNA lesion that may drive the development of CRC and demonstrate the FA pathway’s capacity to repair physiologically relevant ICLs.
Results
Colibactin-induced ICL repair is coupled to DNA replication
To investigate colibactin-induced ICL repair in
Xenopus
egg extracts, we prepared plasmids containing site-specific ICLs generated with either native colibactin (clb) or a synthetic colibactin analog (c742; Fig.
1a
). c742 contains an unsubstituted carbon-carbon linker in place of a central diketone that is susceptible to oxidative cleavage. The stabilized analog produces an ICL that is otherwise structurally identical to a clb-ICL and that can induce cell cycle arrest in human cells
33
. Short oligonucleotide duplexes containing a colibactin alkylation motif were incubated with either c742 or with cultured
pks
+
bacteria. In both cases, cross-links were expected to form between dAs at the second position of a palindromic 5′-A
A
TATT-3′ target sequence (Supplementary Fig.
1a
)
5
,
6
. Following purification, essentially all the duplexes contained a colibactin-induced ICL (Supplementary Fig.
1b
); these were then ligated into ~5.6 kb plasmids. At least 75% of the purified c742-ICL plasmid (pICL
c742
) contained an intact ICL (Supplementary Fig.
1c
). However, only ~50% of the clb-ICL plasmid (pICL
clb
) contained an intact ICL (Supplementary Fig.
1c
), despite preparing the plasmids using highly purified cross-linked oligonucleotides (Supplementary Fig.
1b
). Interestingly, a substantial fraction of the pICL
clb
plasmids contained AP sites and monoadducts, presumably consisting of clb linked to adenine (clb-A) (Supplementary Fig.
1d, e
), which indicates that the clb-ICL can undergo depurination during plasmid preparation. Consistent with previous work, the AP sites in our pICL
clb
preparations are rapidly removed in egg extracts (Supplementary Fig.
1f
)
34
. We therefore infer that replication forks encounter either a clb-ICL or a clb-A monoadduct, but not an AP site, during pICL
clb
replication in egg extracts.
We first asked whether colibactin-induced ICLs are unhooked in egg extracts and whether such unhooking is DNA replication-dependent. pICL
c742
and pICL
clb
were replicated in egg extract, recovered, linearized with a restriction enzyme (HincII), resolved on a denaturing agarose gel, and detected by Southern blotting (Fig.
1c
). Initially, the plasmids were detected as X-shaped structures that migrate slowly due to the presence of a cross-link. The initial accumulation of pICL
clb
X-shaped structures was reduced by the presence of uncross-linked plasmid in our preparation (Supplementary Fig.
1c–f
). During replication in egg extract, the X-shaped structures are resolved into linear species, indicating that the ICL is unhooked (Fig.
1c
and Supplementary Fig.
1g
). Importantly, the conversion of X-shaped structures to linear species was attenuated in extract supplemented with CDC7 inhibitor (PHA-767491), which blocks DNA replication initiation (Fig.
1c
and Supplementary Fig.
1g
)
35
. We conclude that c742-ICL and clb-ICL are unhooked by replication-coupled repair in egg extracts.
pICL
c742
and pICL
clb
were next replicated in egg extract supplemented with [α−
32
P]dCTP, which is incorporated into nascent DNA strands. Replication intermediates were then resolved on a native agarose gel and visualized by autoradiography (Fig.
1d
). For comparison, we also replicated an undamaged plasmid (pCtrl) and plasmids containing either a cisplatin-ICL (pICL
Pt
) or an AP-ICL (pICL
AP
). Whereas replicated pCtrl rapidly accumulated as open circular and supercoiled products, each of the ICL-containing plasmids initially accumulated as slowly migrating “figure 8” intermediates that form when CMG helicases converge and stall on either side of the ICL. In the case of pICL
AP
, the slow figure 8s were rapidly converted into open circular and supercoiled products, indicative of unhooking by the NEIL3 glycosylase
15
. In the case of pICL
c742
and pICL
clb
, the slow figure 8s were first converted into a series of species with intermediate mobilities and later into open circular and supercoiled products. Note that pICL
clb
replication resulted in substantial accumulation of open circular and supercoiled plasmids at even early time points, consistent with the presence of uncross-linked plasmid in this preparation. Interestingly, pICL
c742
and pICL
clb
replication produced intermediates that closely resembled those formed during replication of pICL
Pt
, which is repaired by the FA pathway in egg extracts
36
,
37
. These findings indicate that colibactin-induced ICLs block replication fork progression and activate repair.
In egg extracts, the convergence of replication forks at the ICL triggers TRAIP-dependent polyubiquitylation of CMG
17
. Short ubiquitin chains on CMG are sufficient to recruit the NEIL3 glycosylase, while longer chains enable p97-dependent CMG unloading and activation of the FA pathway. We confirmed that colibactin-induced ICL repair requires fork convergence (Supplementary Fig.
1i
) and so tested whether it also requires CMG unloading. Addition of p97 inhibitor (NMS-873
38
) to pICL
c742
and pICL
clb
replication reactions caused a persistence of slow figure 8s and a reduction in unhooked open circular and supercoiled products (Fig.
1e
), indicating that repair is activated by CMG unloading. Importantly, the absence of unhooking in p97-inhibited extracts implies that c742- and clb-ICLs are not processed by the NEIL3 or AA-ICL pathways, which do not require CMG unloading
14
,
15
. We additionally confirmed that depletion of NEIL3 from extracts has a negligible effect on the repair of pICL
c742
(Supplementary Fig.
1j, k
). We also examined the effect of p97 inhibition on maturation of nascent DNA strands by digesting repair intermediates with restriction enzymes (AflIII and EcoRI) that enable resolution of nascent leading strands on a denaturing sequencing gel (Fig.
1f
). During pICL
c742
and pICL
clb
replication, the nascent leading strands initially stall ~20 to 40 nucleotides (nt) upstream of the ICL due to the footprint of CMG. They are subsequently extended to 1 nt upstream of the expected dA cross-link positions before eventually being converted into full-length extension products. Consistent with a requirement for CMG unloading during pICL
c742
and pICL
clb
repair, p97 inhibitor attenuated extension of the nascent strands from the −20 to −40 stall positions to the −1 position and suppressed the formation of extension products. Note that the effect on extension product accumulation is more pronounced for pICL
c742
than for pICL
clb
, consistent with the presence of uncross-linked plasmid in the pICL
clb
preparation. We conclude that colibactin-induced ICL repair is activated by fork convergence and CMG unloading, suggestive of FA pathway repair.
We noticed that replication of pICL
c742
consistently produced two prominent intermediates that were not observed during replication of pICL
AP
, pICL
Pt

clb

Following ICL unhooking, TLS extends the nascent DNA strands past damaged nucleotides in the template DNA strands. For ICLs formed by nitrogen mustard and cisplatin, TLS is mediated by an insertion polymerase, which inserts a nucleotide opposite the damaged base, and the REV1-Pol ζ complex, which extends the DNA strand
23
. In contrast, REV1 is required for both insertion and extension during repair of ICLs formed by acetaldehyde, psoralen, or AP sites

,
15

c742

4b

clb

1f
). For both pICL
c742
and pICL
clb

4c, d
and Supplementary Fig.
4a
), distinct from the persistence of insertion (0 stall position) products observed during cisplatin-ICL repair in REV1-depleted extracts (Supplementary Fig.
4b–d
)

. Our data, therefore, indicate that REV1 is required for both insertion and extension during TLS past a colibactin-induced ICL remnant. In some experiments, small amounts of insertion products were detected during repair of the c742-ICL that were suppressed by REV1 depletion (e.g., Supplementary Fig.

Discussion
Despite intense interest in colibactin as a driver of colorectal cancer, little is known about the pathways that repair colibactin-induced DNA damage. Our data indicate that colibactin-induced ICL repair is activated upon convergence of replication forks at the lesion and unloading of the replisome (Fig.
8a
). The FA pathway then mediates nucleolytic incisions that release the cross-link and generate a DSB, which is likely repaired by homologous recombination, and an ICL remnant, which is bypassed by TLS. TLS past the unhooked ICL remnant depends on REV1 and Pol κ (most likely in complex with Pol ζ), which together perform both insertion opposite the colibactin-adducted base and extension of the nascent strand. A similar TLS mechanism also enables bypass of colibactin-monoadducts encountered during replication (Fig.
8b
). Bypass of colibactin adducts is mostly error-free, but can introduce T>A point mutations at the alkylated positions. Importantly, we observe no noticeable differences in the unhooking and bypass mechanisms for the c742-ICL and clb-ICL, supporting the use of the c742 analog for investigations into the genotoxic effects of colibactin exposure. Overall, our data provide a comprehensive model for replication-coupled processing of colibactin-induced DNA damage.

Biallelic mutations in any of the 23
FANC
genes linked to FA cause hypersensitivity to ICL-inducing agents
13
. Moreover, the biochemical activities of FANC proteins comprise a common replication-coupled pathway that enables ICL repair. These insights have led to the presumption that FA is caused by a failure to repair endogenous ICLs. However, a key outstanding question concerns the identities of the cognate endogenous ICLs that engage the FA pathway and presumably drive progression of bone marrow failure and cancer in FA patients. Mutations in the FA pathway strongly synergize with mutations in
ALDH2
and
ADH5
, which enable detoxification of acetaldehyde and formaldehyde, respectively
25
,
26
, implying that unrepaired ICLs produced by endogenous reactive aldehydes cause FA. However, the specific chemical structures of aldehyde-induced ICLs that arise in human cells and drive progression of FA remain elusive. To our knowledge, the clb-ICL is the only naturally occurring ICL with both genetic and physical evidence to substantiate its formation in vivo
3
–
8
. Our data therefore demonstrate that the FA pathway repairs an ICL that is likely to arise at some point over the lifetime of most individuals.
While our data reveal that the FA pathway promotes resistance to colibactin-induced ICLs, it is unclear whether colibactin contributes to the etiology or progression of FA. We are unaware of any evidence linking
pks
+
bacteria to bone marrow failure, and current data do not suggest that FA patients are at elevated risk for CRC, though sporadic cases have been reported
46
. Interestingly, the colibactin-associated mutational signature has been detected in squamous cell carcinomas, a cancer for which FA patients are at dramatically increased risk
47
. A recent genomic analysis of squamous cell carcinomas from FA patients did not identify colibactin-associated SBSs or single-nucleotide deletions
48
. However, it may be that colibactin-induced DNA damage manifests different mutational signatures in individuals lacking a functional FA pathway. In FA patients, colibactin exposure may instead produce more complex structural variants at AT-rich colibactin alkylation hotspots due to alternative processing of ICLs. The colibactin-associated mutational signature has also been detected in cancers derived from additional tissue types
47
. Future studies are therefore warranted to determine whether FA patients are at increased risk for complications arising due to colonization by
pks
+
bacteria.
Colibactin exhibits a striking specificity for the N3 position of dA in AT-rich motifs
10
. The three-dimensional structure of a colibactin-induced ICL implicates hydrogen bonding and electrostatic interactions within the relatively narrow minor groove of AT-rich DNA in the specificity of colibactin-ICL formation
10
. Both monoalkylation by colibactin and nucleolytic unhooking of a colibactin-induced ICL generate similar adducts comprising an N3 alkylated dA (in the latter case, the colibactin scaffold may be further linked to the short oligonucleotide generated by unhooking incisions). In general, TLS past minor groove adducts is thought to depend primarily on the polymerase activity of Pol κ. Pol κ-deficient cells are hypersensitive to genotoxins that induce minor groove adducts (e.g., illudin S and mitomycin C), and Pol κ has been shown to efficiently extend DNA primers past
N
2
-dG adducts (e.g., benzo[a]pyrene-
N
2
-dG) and N3-dA adducts (e.g., 3-deaza-3-methyl-dA) in vitro
49
,
50
. Additionally, TLS past a p3d-Phen-A adduct in egg extract was recently reported to depend on Pol κ polymerase activity, but not on REV1
42
. It is therefore somewhat surprising that the bypass of colibactin-induced adducts requires REV1 but not Pol κ polymerase activity. Despite having a catalytically active site that can accommodate minor groove adducts
51
, Pol κ might be inhibited by the much larger size of the colibactin adducts (clb-A molecular weight is ~900 Da). Colibactin may also make additional contacts to DNA in the minor groove that impede insertion by Pol κ. Finally, we note that previous studies have examined bypass of N3-dA adducts using stabilizing 3-deaza-substituted dA analogs that may not completely recapitulate the effects of N3 alkylation
42
.
Our data also indicate that Pol η promotes the approach of nascent leading strands to within 1 nt of a colibactin-induced ICL. Based on the timing of the nascent strand approach, we infer that Pol η helps to extend the nascent strands after CMG unloading and before FANCI-FANCD2-dependent incisions unhook the ICL. REV1 and Pol κ then act together to enable insertion opposite the alkylated base and subsequent extension past the lesion. Similar coordination between Pol η and REV1-Pol ζ has been observed during bypass of DNA-protein cross-links, cisplatin-induced intrastrand cross-links, and UV-induced 6,4 photoproducts
52
–
54
. In these cases, Pol η normally performs insertion of a nucleotide opposite the lesion while REV1-Pol ζ performs the extension step. In the case of colibactin-ICLs, however, Pol η appears unable to perform insertion, even when REV1 is absent. It may be that the structure of the colibactin-ICL blocks insertion by Pol η. In the context of model ICL duplexes, strand displacement synthesis and insertion by Pol η was shown to be inhibited by a non-distorting ICL, resulting in an accumulation of −1 stall products
55
. The relatively non-distorting colibactin-ICL may also suppress insertion by Pol η, necessitating insertion by Pol κ-REV1-Pol ζ once unhooking has occurred
10
.
Mutational signatures associated with colibactin exposure include predominantly T>C SBSs at AT-rich hexanucleotide sequences and single-nucleotide T deletions at T-homopolymer sequences
4
–
6
. T>G and T>A SBSs are also detected, though less frequently than T>C mutations. Our data provide some insight as to the origin of these mutational signatures. Bypass of both unhooked colibactin-induced ICL remnants and monoadducts can introduce a T>A point mutation through the insertion of dA opposite an alkylated dA. This immediately suggests that the T>A mutations observed in cells, organoids, and colonic crypts exposed to colibactin arise through Pol κ-REV1-Pol ζ-dependent TLS past colibactin adducts. This subset of colibactin-associated SBSs may therefore represent a mutational signature for clb-ICL repair by the FA pathway.
How then might the more prevalent T>C mutations arise? A trivial explanation is that Pol κ-REV1-Pol ζ-dependent TLS past a colibactin adduct produces different mutations in frogs and humans due to divergence of the TLS polymerases between species. Alternatively, T>C mutations might be produced through distinct ICL repair mechanisms or through repair of distinct colibactin-induced DNA lesions. ICLs can be unhooked through replication-independent mechanisms involving mismatch repair or transcription-coupled nucleotide excision repair
45
,
56
. Both pathways would generate a ssDNA gap at the lesion and require TLS past an ICL remnant in the remaining strand. Interestingly, the catalytic activity of Pol κ is required for replication-independent ICL repair
45
. Colibactin-induced ICLs can decompose into DSBs through depurination and AP site cleavage, requiring DNA end-joining. In such instances, the activities of alternative polymerases such as Pol λ, Pol μ, or Pol θ might be required to generate compatible DNA ends for ligation
57
. Thus, the colibactin-associated T>N mutation spectrum could reflect an amalgamation of TLS polymerase activities that act in different contexts.
When ICL unhooking or TLS is inhibited, colibactin-induced DNA lesions appear to be bypassed by a mechanism that tends to introduce deletions. We propose that replication forks that undergo persistent stalling at a colibactin-induced ICL undergo breakage and collapse into DSBs that are repaired through an error-prone end-joining pathway, such as Pol θ-mediated end-joining (TMEJ)
58
. Similarly, Pol θ might enable microhomology-mediated gap skipping at colibactin-induced monoadducts when TLS is inhibited
59
. Consistent with this interpretation, we observe that the vast majority of the deletions detected in our sequencing data encompass at least a portion of the colibactin alkylation hotspot (Fig.
6b
). Such deletion structures are explainable by Pol θ-dependent annealing and extension of 3′ ends at sites of microhomology. It will therefore be interesting to determine whether inhibition of Pol θ and other end-joining factors influences frequencies and structures of deletions produced during colibactin-induced ICL repair. Going forward, it will also be important to examine the mutagenicity of colibactin exposure in cells carrying mutations in
FANC
genes, Pol κ, Pol ζ, Pol θ, and other TLS polymerases, and alternative ICL repair pathways. Such experiments will be critical for unambiguously mapping colibactin-associated mutational signatures to specific DNA damage tolerance mechanisms.

Replication reactions
Plasmid replication reactions in
Xenopus
egg extracts were performed essentially as previously described
62
. Briefly, HSS was thawed and supplemented with 20 mM phosphocreatine, 2 mM ATP, 5 µg mL
−1
creatine phosphokinase, and 3 µg mL
−1
nocodazole. Plasmids were added to the HSS mix to a concentration of 7.5 ng µL
−1
and incubated at room temperature for 30 min to enable licensing. For assays involving LacR acting as a replication block, plasmids were pre-incubated with 14 µM biotinylated LacI for 1 h at room temperature before being added to HSS. Where indicated, the licensing mix was supplemented with 167–333 nM 3000 Ci mmoL
−1
[α−
32
P]dCTP and/or 400 nM rGeminin. NPE mix was made with 50% NPE, 20 mM phosphocreatine, 2 mM ATP, 5 µg mL
-1
creatine phosphokinase, and 4 mM DTT in ELB. Where indicated, the NPE mix was with 50 µM PHA-767491 HCl or 300 µM NMS-873. Replication was initiated by the addition of 2 volumes of NPE mix to 1 volume of licensing mix. Where indicated, 10 mM IPTG was added 15 min into the replication time course to dissociate LacI from the plasmid. For samples analyzed by APE1 digestion, HSS and NPE mixes were combined before adding the plasmid (i.e., replication origins were not licensed in the HSS mix). For analysis on native agarose gels, 1 µL samples of the reaction were removed at indicated time points and quenched by addition to 6 µL of replication stop mix (80 mM Tris-HCl [pH 8.0], 8 mM EDTA, 0.13% phosphoric acid, 10% ficoll, 5% SDS, 0.1% bromophenol blue). After all time points were quenched, samples were digested with 1.25 mg mL
−1
proteinase K for 60 min at 37 °C, and replication intermediates and products were resolved on 0.8% agarose, 1X TBE gels. Gels were dried and visualized by phosphorimaging. Autoradiograms were imaged with a Typhoon FLA 9500 (GE Healthcare) using the FujiFilm FLA 9500 user interface v.1.1 and analyzed using Image Lab v.6.4.0. For Southern blots and nascent strand analysis on sequencing gels, 4 µL samples of the reaction were removed at indicated time points and quenched by addition to 40 µL of clear replication stop mix (50 mM Tris-HCl [pH 8.8], 0.5% SDS, 25 mM EDTA). After all time points were quenched, samples were digested with 200 µg mL
−1
RNAse A for 30 min at 37 °C and then with 1 mg mL
−1
proteinase K for 60 min at 37 °C. Samples were adjusted to 200 µL with 10 mM Tris-HCl [pH 8.8], extracted twice with phenol:chloroform:isoamyl alcohol (25:24:1; pH 8.0) and once with chloroform, and ethanol precipitated. DNA was resuspended in 10 µL of 10 mM Tris-HCl (pH 8.8), 50 mM NaCl, 1 mM MgCl
2
(for c742-ICL and clb-ICL plasmids) or 10 mM Tris-HCl pH 8.5 (for all other plasmids) and stored at −20 °C (or −80 °C for plasmids intended for unhooking assays). For samples analyzed by APE1 digestion, 3 µL of recovered DNA were incubated with 1 U APE1 in 1X NEBuffer 4 (50 mM potassium acetate, 20 mM Tris-acetate, 10 mM magnesium acetate, 1 mM DTT; pH 7.9) in a total volume of 10 µL at 37 °C for 60 min. Samples were subsequently run on a 0.8% agarose, 1X TBE, 0.5 µg mL
−1
ethidium bromide gel and visualized with a UV transilluminator.
Southern blotting
Southern blotting was performed essentially as previously described
37
. Briefly, samples were replicated as described above, and 3 µL of recovered DNA were incubated with 5 U HincII in 1X NEBuffer rCutsmart (50 mM potassium acetate, 20 mM Tris-acetate, 10 mM magnesium acetate, 100 µg mL
−1
recombinant albumin; pH 7.9) in a total volume of 5 µL at 37 °C for 60 min. Following digestion, 5 µL of 50 mM Tris-HCl (pH 8.8), 50 mM NaCl, 10 mM EDTA, and 2 µL of 6X alkaline loading buffer (300 mM NaOH, 6 mM EDTA, 18% ficoll, 0.25% xylene cyanol, 0.15% bromocresol green) was added to each sample. The DNA was resolved on a denaturing 0.8% agarose, 50 mM NaOH, 1 mM EDTA gel for 20 h at 1.25 V cm
−1
. After running was complete, the gel was incubated in 0.25 M HCl for 20 min and in 0.4 M NaOH, 3 M NaCl for 60 min. Downward capillary transfer onto an Invitrogen BrightStar-Plus positively charged nylon membrane was performed overnight in 0.4 M NaOH, 1.5 M NaCl. The membrane was subsequently washed with 4X SSC buffer (0.6 M NaCl, 60 mM sodium citrate; pH 7.0) for 5 min, and the DNA was cross-linked to the membrane via 265 nm UV irradiation (120,000 µJ cm
−2
) with a UVP HybriLinker Oven. The membrane was then incubated with 15 mL ULTRAhyb Ultrasensitive Hybridization Buffer (Invitrogen) for 1–2 h at 42 °C. During this prehybridization, a radioactive probe was made using 50 ng of linearized pCtrl and the Prime-a-Gene Labeling System kit (Promega) following the manufacturer’s instructions. The probe was added to the hybridization tube and incubated with the membrane at 42 °C for 18 h. After hybridization, the membrane was washed twice with 1X SSC, 0.7% SDS at 42 °C for 10–20 min per wash and twice with 0.1X SSC, 0.7% SDS that was pre-heated to 75 °C for 10–20 min per wash. The membrane was dried briefly on blotting paper and visualized by phosphorimaging as described above.
Nascent strand analysis
Nascent strand analysis was performed essentially as previously described
36
. Briefly, samples were replicated as described above, and 2 µL of recovered DNA were incubated with 2 U AflIII and 4 U of either EcoRI or BamHI in 50 mM Tris-HCl (pH 8), 100 mM NaCl, 10 mM MgCl
2
in a total volume of 5 µL at 37 °C for 3 h. Reactions were stopped by adding 5 µL of Invitrogen Gel Loading Buffer II. Primers for sequencing ladders were radiolabeled by incubating 200 nM sequencing primer with 200 nM [γ−
32
P]ATP and 20 U T4 polynucleotide kinase (NEB) in 1X T4 PNK reaction buffer (70 mM Tris-HCl, 10 mM MgCl
2
, 5 mM DTT; pH 7.6) in a total volume of 50 µL for 30 min at 37 °C. T4 PNK was inactivated by heating at 95 °C for 2 min, and the unincorporated radionucleotides were removed using a Micro Bio-Spin column (Bio-Rad) per the manufacturer’s instructions. Sequencing ladders were made using the Thermo Sequenase Cycle Sequencing Kit: 0.5 pmol of radiolabeled primer mixed with 175 ng of pCtrl, 2 µL of reaction buffer, and 2 µL of Sequenase in a total volume of 17.5. 4 µL of this reaction mix was then added to 4 µL of ddA, ddG, ddC, or ddT termination mixes, and the reactions were incubated on a PCR block at 95 °C for 3 min, followed by 50 cycles of 95 °C for 30 s, 60 °C for 60 s, and 72 °C for 90 s. Eight microliters of Invitrogen Gel Loading Buffer II were added to each reaction, and the sequencing ladders were stored at −20 °C until use. Immediately before loading, all samples were heated at 75 °C for 5 min and snap-cooled in an ice water bath. DNA was resolved on a 7% acrylamide/bis (19:1), 8 M urea, 0.8X glycerol tolerant gel (GTG) buffer (71 mM Tris-HCl, 23 mM taurine, 0.4 mM EDTA) gel. Sequencing gels were dried and visualized by phosphorimaging as described above.

Plasmid pulldowns for the purpose of mass spectrometry were performed essentially as previously described

Briefly, 6 µL of M-280 Streptavidin Dynabeads (Invitrogen) per time point were washed three times with 50 mM Tris-HCl (pH 7.5), 150 mM NaCl, 0.02% Tween-20, and 1 mM EDTA (pH 8.0) and subsequently incubated in the same buffer supplemented with 2 pmol of biotinylated LacI per µL of beads for 40 min at room temperature on a rotator wheel. The beads were washed four times with pulldown buffer (2.5 mM MgCl
2
, 50 mM KCl, 10 mM HEPES, 250 mM sucrose, 0.25 mg mL
−1
BSA, 0.02% Tween-20), divided into 40 µL aliquots, and stored on ice. Replication reactions were performed as described above, except extracts were supplemented with 40 µg mL
−1
RNAse A and 10 U µL
−1
RNAse T1, and plasmids were replicated at a final concentration of 5 ng µL
−1
in extracts. At the indicated times, 8 µL of each reaction was quenched into 40 µL of Dynabeads (with four replicates for each time point) and immediately incubated on a rotator wheel for 30 min at 4 °C to enable binding of the plasmid’s
lacO
array to the LacI-coated beads. After the incubation, the beads were washed twice at 4 °C with 2.5 mM MgCl
2
, 50 mM KCl, 10 mM HEPES, 250 mM sucrose, 0.03% Tween-20, and once with 2.5 mM MgCl
2
, 50 mM KCl, 10 mM HEPES, 250 mM sucrose. For each time point, the beads for one of the replicates were suspended in 10 µL of 1X Laemmli loading buffer and analyzed by immunoblotting. The buffer was aspirated from the beads, and they were resuspended in 50 µL of 8 M urea in 50 mM HEPES-KOH (pH 8.0). Subsequent steps were performed at room temperature unless otherwise indicated. Samples were incubated with 20 mM DTT for 15 min, supplemented with chloroacetamide to 58 mM, and incubated at 1200 rpm on a Thermomixer for 40 min (covered in foil to protect from light). Samples were then incubated with 1.5 µg Lys-C at 1400 rpm on a Thermomixer for 150 min. Following the incubation, supernatants containing the eluted peptides were separated from the beads on a magnetic rack and transferred to fresh tubes (~60 µL of supernatant per sample). Samples were adjusted to 200 µL with 50 mM ammonium bicarbonate and incubated with 2.5 µg of trypsin at 30 °C overnight. Digestions were terminated by adding 20 µL of 10% TFA (trifluoroacetic acid) and adjusted to 0.5 M NaCl by adding 74 µL of 2 M NaCl. Stage tips were prepared by dispensing two C18 disks into 200 µL pipette tips with a blunt needle and spinning at 500 ×
g
for 3 min to pack the disks. All subsequent stage tip spins were also performed at 500 ×
g
for 3 min. Stage tips were activated by spinning with 100 µL 50% acetonitrile (ACN) and equilibrated by spinning with 100 µL 0.1% TFA. Samples were spun at 8000 ×
g
for 10 min to pellet any undigested DNA debris. Eighty-five microliters of supernatant were applied to stage tips and spun; this step was repeated two more times, leaving ~40 µL of each sample behind to avoid disturbing the pellet. Stage tips were washed twice with 100 µL of 0.1% TFA, and peptides were eluted twice with 50 µL of 50% ACN, 0.1% TFA. g

LC-MS/MS analysis was performed with an EASY-nLC 1200 (Thermo Fisher Scientific, San Jose, CA) coupled to a Q Exactive HF hybrid quadrupole-Orbitrap mass spectrometer (Thermo Fisher Scientific, San Jose, CA). Peptides were separated on an Aurora UHPLC Column (25 cm × 75 μm, 1.7 μm C18, AUR3-25075C18, Ion Opticks) with a flow rate of 0.35 μL min
−1
for a total duration of 75 min and ionized at 1.6 kV in the positive ion mode. The gradient was composed of 6% solvent B (3.5 min), 6–25% B (42 min), 25–40% B (14.5 min), and 40–98% B (15 min); solvent A: 2% ACN and 0.2% formic acid in water; solvent B: 80% ACN and 0.2% formic acid. MS1 scans were acquired at a resolution of 60,000 from 375 to 1500
m
/
z
, AGC target 3E6, and maximum injection time 15 ms. The 12 most abundant ions in MS2 scans were acquired at a resolution of 30,000, AGC target 1E5, maximum injection time 60 ms, and a normalized collision energy of 28. Dynamic exclusion was set to 30 s, and ions with charges of +1, +7, +8, and >+8 were excluded. The temperature of the ion transfer tube was 275 °C, and the S-lens RF level was set to 60.
Proteomic data processing
Label-free quantification (LFQ) of protein abundances was performed with the MaxLFQ algorithm implemented in MaxQuant (MQ v2.3.1.0)
63
–
65
. The analysis used default settings with match between runs functionality enabled. RAW data were searched against an in silico tryptic digested protein reference database based on the 10.1 version of the
Xenopus laevis
genome downloaded from Xenbase (
https://wuehr.scholar.princeton.edu/sites/g/files/toruqf2761/files/xenla_10_1_xenbase.fasta_.txt
). The maximum missed cleavages were set to 2. Dynamic modifications were set to oxidation on methionine (M, +15.995 Da) and protein N-terminal acetylation (+42.011 Da). Carbamidomethylation on cysteine residues (C, +57.021 Da) was set as a fixed modification. Protein quantification was performed using the built-in LFQ algorithm. The data have been deposited to the ProteomeXchange Consortium via the PRIDE partner repository with the dataset identifier PXD055646
66
.
The Perseus software platform (v.2.1.2.0) was used for data filtering and normalization
67
. Potential contaminant proteins, reverse database protein hits, proteins identified only by modification site, and proteins that were not quantified in at least one replicate group were removed from the analysis. LFQ intensities were log2-transformed, and samples were median-normalized. Missing abundance values were imputed from a downshifted normal distribution with default parameters defined in Perseus. For heatmap visualization, normalized abundances were averaged within biological replicate groups and standardized. The R package
limma
was used for statistical analysis of protein abundances
68
. Differential expression
p
values from empirical Bayes moderated t-testing of the log2-transformed protein ratios were adjusted for multiple hypothesis testing with the Benjamini-Hochberg procedure
69
.

Preparation of next-generation sequencing libraries
In preparation for NGS, plasmids were replicated as described above. After extraction and ethanol precipitation, samples were resuspended to a concentration of approximately 10–15 ng µL
−1
. Four microliters of recovered DNA were mixed with 200 nM each of forward and reverse primer (see Supplementary Table
1
), 200 µM dNTPs, and 2 units of Phusion High-Fidelity DNA Polymerase (NEB) in 1X Phusion HF buffer to a total volume of 100 µL. Amplicons were generated by PCR with initial heating to 98 °C for 30 s, followed by 18 cycles of 98 °C for 10 s, 55 °C for 30 s, and 72 °C for 30 s, and a final incubation at 72 °C for 10 min. The amplified DNA was purified with a QIAquick PCR Purification Kit (Qiagen) per the manufacturer’s instructions and inspected on a 0.8% agarose, 1X TBE gel visualized with SYBR Gold to confirm amplification. Samples were then submitted to Azenta for paired-end NGS (Illumina MiSeq, 2 × 250 bp).
NGS data processing
Raw sequencing reads were cropped to 150 bp using Trimmomatic (v0.39) to avoid later merging failures due to sequencing errors at the ends of amplicons
70
. Reads were then processed using SIQ (v1.8) with long-read analysis enabled and otherwise default settings, and the SIQPlotteR web tool was used to generate plots
71
. pICL
clb
contains a single C-C mismatch designed to distinguish reads derived from the two parental strands. These were not deconvoluted in our analysis; instead, the SBS corresponding to the C-C mismatch was manually removed from the SIQ output for pICL
clb
data sets.
